title: A production and trade comparison
context: With fixed resources, A can make 30 solar panels or 10 pumps; B can make 20 panels or 10 pumps. Assume linear frontiers.
prompts: Calculate opportunity cost of a pump for each.
Assign comparative advantages.
Offer mutually beneficial terms of trade.
Distinguish a movement along a frontier from an outward shift.
criteria: A gives up 3 panels per pump; B gives up 2.
B has comparative advantage in pumps; A in panels.
A rate strictly between 2 and 3 panels per pump can benefit both.
Reallocation moves along a frontier; new resources or technology can move it outward.

title: Reading economic indicators
context: A fictional economy has C = 400, I = 100, G = 120, X = 60 and M = 80. Nominal GDP is 600 and the deflator is 120. There are 90 employed and 10 unemployed active job seekers.
prompts: Calculate spending-side GDP.
Calculate real GDP from the nominal value and deflator.
Calculate unemployment.
Explain one reason these figures are insufficient to measure welfare.
criteria: Unemployment = 10 / 100 × 100 = 10%.
Distribution, nonmarket activity and environmental quality are among the missing welfare dimensions.

title: Closing a recessionary gap
context: Output is 900 and potential output is 1000. MPC is 0.75. Use a fixed-price closed-economy multiplier with no taxes, imports or crowding out.
prompts: Identify the gap and show it on an AD–AS graph.
Find the simple spending multiplier.
Calculate the G increase needed in this model.
Explain one reason the actual policy effect could differ.
criteria: There is a recessionary gap of 100; show initial output left of LRAS.
Multiplier = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
Required G increase is 100 / 4 = 25.
Price changes, import leakage, timing and interest-rate responses can change the result; do not claim a guaranteed forecast.

title: Policy under ample reserves
context: A central bank has ample reserves and lowers its administered interest rates. Hold risk, expectations and other policy settings fixed.
prompts: Identify the intended short-term market-rate direction.
Trace a possible investment and AD response.
Explain why an open-market purchase alone need not move the rate much in this regime.
Distinguish the real loanable-funds rate from the nominal money-market rate.
criteria: Short-term rates tend to fall as administered rates fall.
Lower borrowing costs can raise investment and shift AD right, conditional on other determinants.
Reserve demand can be relatively flat in the ample-reserves range.
A real rate adjusts for inflation; diagrams must state the rate and market rather than mixing the two.

title: Debt and longer-run effects
context: Outlays are 320, revenues 280 and initial debt 1000. Ignore other debt adjustments. Assume a closed loanable-funds market with unchanged saving behavior.
prompts: Calculate the deficit and new debt.
Show how extra public borrowing can affect the real rate.
Explain possible crowding out.
Describe a separate policy channel that could raise long-run capacity.
criteria: Deficit = 40; simplified new debt = 1040.
Using the borrowing-demand convention, demand shifts right and the real rate rises.
Higher rates can lower private investment and future capital accumulation.
Productive education, infrastructure or research can raise capacity; assess effectiveness and opportunity costs rather than guaranteeing growth.

title: Currency appreciation
context: The rate moves from 0.8 to 1 foreign unit per domestic unit. A domestic item keeps a price of 50 domestic units. Assume flexible exchange rates and other goods prices fixed.
prompts: Identify which currency appreciates.
Calculate the foreign buyer’s cost before and after.
Explain the usual net-export and AD channel.
Explain how a higher relative domestic real rate could help cause this exchange movement.
criteria: The domestic currency appreciates in the stated quotation.
Foreign cost rises from 40 to 50 foreign units.
Domestic exports become less competitive and imports more attractive, tending to reduce NX and AD.
Higher relative real returns can attract capital inflows and raise demand for domestic currency, holding risk and expectations fixed.
